tagline.text: The Philippines' tuna capital, where dawn fish markets pile high with tuna

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (rarely affected by typhoons), Tuna Festival in September

image.credit: Jay Morales, DA-AFID / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Michael E. Peligro / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A port city in southern Mindanao on Sarangani Bay, the tuna capital where more sashimi-grade tuna comes ashore than anywhere else in the Philippines. Take in the dawn fish market, enjoy cheap and fresh tuna dishes, and use the city as a gateway to Lake Sebu and Sarangani's beaches.

General Santos, often called GenSan, is a port city of about 720,000 people set inside Sarangani Bay at Mindanao's southern tip. Originally the land of the B'laan people, its old name Dadiangas came from a tree once common in the area. The city began in
when General Paulino Santos led settlers here from Luzon to found the settlement; it was later named in his honor and became a city in
The city's nickname is the
Tuna Capital of the Philippines

. At the General Santos Fish Port Complex in Barangay Tambler to the south, yellowfin and skipjack tuna caught in the Celebes Sea and the Pacific are unloaded every day, and the city produces more sashimi-grade tuna than anywhere else in the country. Its total catch also ranks second nationwide after Navotas in Manila, and several tuna canning factories are clustered here.

General Santos is one of the driest regions in the Philippines, and with typhoons rarely passing through, the weather stays stable year-round. The city is also famous as the place where world boxing hero Manny Pacquiao grew up, and many visitors come to see his mansion and related sights. Downtown has the beachfront Queen Tuna Park, the General Paulino Santos Museum, and large shopping malls, while to the north lie Mount Matutum and sprawling pineapple plantations.

It's not a city packed with tourist attractions, but the chance to eat the cheapest, freshest tuna anywhere is reason enough to stop by. With an airport of its own, it also serves as a starting point for trips around southern Mindanao — to Lake Sebu, Lake Holon, and Gumasa Beach in Sarangani — making it worth recommending to food-loving travelers and anyone planning a southern Mindanao loop.

blocks.title: Watching the dawn tuna auction at the fish port

children.text: From the earliest hours of dawn, the fish port buzzes with tuna being unloaded from boats, weighed, and auctioned. The sight of rows of tuna as tall as a person is unique to this city, and there are entry rules, so follow the guidance at the gate.

In a single meal you can try grilled tuna jaw (panga), grilled tuna belly, kinilaw tossed with vinegar and ginger, sinuglaw (grilled pork mixed with kinilaw), and even tuna sashimi. You can enjoy fresh tuna at prices far cheaper than in Korea.

A beachfront park stretching along Sarangani Bay, where in the evening locals gather to watch the sun set behind the mountains across the bay. It's a good spot for a walk, a jog, and street-food snacks.
Held every year from
late August to September 5
around the city's charter anniversary, the Tuna Festival features street parades, tuna cooking competitions, and seafood exhibits. The whole city has a festive buzz during this period.
Held in
February
, the Kalilangan Festival celebrates the cultures of the many settler groups and indigenous tribes who call the city home, with traditional dances and costume processions.

A small museum introducing the history of the settlers who founded the city, B'laan culture, and the development of the tuna industry. Understanding the city's background makes visiting the fish port that much more interesting.

Manny Pacquiao's mansion and facilities bearing his name are scattered around the city. It's a great chance for boxing fans to snap a photo, and you'll get a sense of just how proud locals are of him.

1 hour 50 minutes–2 hours

1 hour 20 minutes
, and some cities such as Iloilo also have direct flights.
The airport is on the northern outskirts of the city, about
20–30 minutes
by taxi to downtown, for around
. You can also take a jeepney from outside the airport toward the bus terminal for a cheaper ride.
From the Davao City Overland Transport Terminal (DCOTT) in Ecoland, an air-conditioned bus to General Santos via Digos takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–4 hours
, for around
. Yellow Bus Line is the most widely used, and direct trips are faster.
From Koronadal it takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
(about
). Long-distance buses arrive at the Bulaong Integrated Bus Terminal north of the city.

There are occasional passenger ferries linking General Santos to places like Davao, but sailings are infrequent and schedules change often, so flying or taking the bus is more practical for travelers.
Among regular passenger ships, 2GO runs a Manila–Davao–General Santos–Iloilo loop once a week (departing Manila on Wednesday). Some piers at Makar Wharf were damaged by the
June 2026
earthquake and are operating with limits, so check the sailing schedule with the shipping company first.
White metered taxis are plentiful and convenient, and you can reach most of downtown for close to the base fare. Tricycles, multicabs, and jeepneys run about
for a short trip.
Public transport is scarce for a dawn visit to the fish port, so arrange a time with a taxi driver the day before, or ask your accommodation to arrange a vehicle.

General Santos gets under about 1,000mm of rain a year on average, one of the driest regions in the Philippines, and sits outside the typhoon path, making it good for travel virtually year-round. Temperatures run hot around
all year, and even the relatively rainy
May–October
usually sees no more than brief afternoon showers. The midday sun is very strong, so plan outdoor activities for early morning and sunset.
If you'd like to catch a festival, aim for the Tuna Festival (
late August to September 5
) or the Kalilangan Festival (
February

). Accommodation fills up fast during festival periods, and roads are closed on parade days, so book ahead and leave some slack in your schedule. Tuna fishing continues year-round, but the volume landed can vary with weather and fishing conditions.

Accommodation clusters around downtown, near the malls, and along the road to the airport. Options range from pension houses and guesthouses at about
a night to business hotels around
and mid-range hotels from about

. If you're planning a dawn visit to the fish port, lodging near the southern Tambler area is convenient, and if you're continuing on to Lake Sebu, somewhere near the northern bus terminal works better.

In this city, it's tuna or nothing. Charcoal-grilled tuna jaw (panga) and belly, kinilaw tossed with vinegar, ginger, and onion, sinuglaw (grilled pork mixed with kinilaw), and a sour sinigang soup made from tuna tail and bones are the signature dishes. There are many tuna-specialist restaurants and food parks around the port and downtown, and container-converted food courts let you try a variety of dishes cheaply. Many places price by cut and weight, so check the price before ordering.
The fish port is liveliest between
4 and 7 AM
. You may be asked for ID, and visit rules can change, so follow the guidance at the gatehouse and be careful not to get in the way of the work.
The floor of the fish port is very slippery with water, ice, and fish oil. Wear non-slip shoes you don't mind getting wet, and avoid white clothing.
Popular cuts like the jaw sell out first. Eating lunch a little early makes it easier to get the cut you want.
The midday sun is strong and the air dry. Always carry sunscreen, a hat, and water.
If you're planning to head to Lake Sebu or Lake Holon, leave General Santos early in the morning and schedule your trip to arrive before dark.
Processed goods like dried tuna, canned tuna, tuna sausages, and tuna snacks are light, long-lasting, and make good gifts.
The schedules of the Tuna Festival and the Kalilangan Festival, and news of events such as fish port tours, can be found on the
official GenSan tourism website
run by the city tourism office.

Downtown General Santos is relatively stable, but travel advisories are in effect for some parts of Mindanao. Before you go, check the latest travel advisories from your home country, and avoid traveling to the outskirts late at night.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake off Maasim, Sarangani on
June 8, 2026
damaged about 30% of the buildings in the city. The airport resumed commercial operations on
June 15

and the large shopping malls reopened one by one after inspection, but the fish port complex closed part of the market building and operated with limits. Aftershocks continue, so check the emergency exits at your lodging and confirm in advance whether the facilities you plan to visit are operating.
Watch for pickpockets in crowded spots such as festival parades, malls, and the bus terminal.
Eat raw-fish dishes like kinilaw and sashimi at busy restaurants with fast turnover. If you're unsure about hygiene, it's safer to choose a cooked dish.
Make sure taxis use the meter, and negotiate flat fares in advance with touts at the airport and terminal.
The water off Queen Tuna Park has dark sand, can get choppy, and water quality isn't consistent. Save your swimming for the beaches of Sarangani.
Walking around at midday carries a risk of heatstroke. Take breaks at malls or cafes as you go.
